title: Token Reclamation and Cold-Cache Resuscitation: Operator Playbook
author: Priya Nambiar
summary: A pragmatic operator playbook to reclaim leaked/stranded request tokens, repair and warm LLM KV/prefix caches after extended cold periods, and restore service SLOs while minimizing cost impact. Includes monitoring checks, fast remediation steps, safe rollbacks, and post-run analysis templates.
body:
Summary

This playbook provides step-by-step guidance for platform operators to: (1) identify and reclaim token leaks or stranded compute attributed to stalled/gone-away clients, (2) resuscitate model prefix/KV caches after prolonged cold periods (e.g., single-tenant idleness, regional failovers), and (3) safely ramp the cache warm-up to meet latency SLOs without unbounded cost.

Context and motivation

- Problem space: long-lived KV/prefix caches and batching/queueing optimizations significantly reduce per-token cost and latency, but they can be underutilized after long idle windows, or corrupted/fragmented due to partial failures. Token accounting mismatches (leaked tokens) can also cause billing anomalies and resource exhaustion.
- Impact: tail latency SLO breaches (P99 > 500ms), elevated GPU time with low throughput, unexpected overprovisioning/evictions, and customer billing disputes.
- Goal: restore functional caches and correct token accounting within 30–90 minutes while limiting incremental GPU spend to a configurable budget.

When to run this playbook

- Alerts firing: "kv-cache-hit-rate < 20% for 10m", "P99 inference latency > target for 15m", "token-burst-forensics suspicious-token-duration > 5m"
- Symptoms: surge of cold-starts on specific model shards/regions, rising unit-cost per token, repeated cache rehydration failures, or tenant complaints about sluggish responses after failover.
- Preconditions: ensure no active global deploy/rollout that would confound the runbook. If a rollout is in progress, coordinate with the deployment owner.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: Platform Operator on shift (eng-platform).
- Secondary escalation: Serving Runtime on-call (eng-serving-runtime) if kernel-level or GPU errors observed.
- Time-to-escalate: escalate to secondary if remediation steps 1–3 completed with no improvement after 30 minutes.

SLOs and run acceptance criteria

- Target for remediation window: reduce P99 latency back to baseline within 60 minutes for affected route(s).
- Cost cap: incremental GPU spend for warmup must not exceed configured burst budget (default: $500 per region for emergency warmups) unless approved by capacity owner.
- Post-fix: no residual token accounting anomalies older than 10 minutes.

Monitoring and dashboards to consult

1) Primary dashboards (operator console):
- Model shard heatmap (qps, prefix-cache hit-rate, kv-cache size)
- Token-forensics timeline (per-tenant token durations, open token sessions)
- Cost burn and GPU utilization per region
- Tail-latency waterfall (queueing vs kernel time)

2) Alerts and thresholds to watch:
- kv-cache-hit-rate < 20% for 10m (severity P1)
- p99-latency-route > 2x target for 15m (severity P1)
- token-session-duration > 5m for sessions > 100k tokens (severity P2)

Immediate remediation checklist (fast path)

IMPORTANT: Run through steps sequentially unless you identify a clear single root cause. Note commands are examples — use the operator CLI with your region and cluster flags.

1) Verify scope and list affected shards/tenants

- Action: Open Model Shard Heatmap, filter for low cache-hit-rate and high P99.
- Command (example): redwood operator shards list --region us-west-2 --filter "cache_hit_rate<0.2"

2) Isolate suspected leaked token sessions

- Action: Query token-forensics for long-lived sessions on the affected shard.
- Command (example): redwood telemetry token-sessions query --since 30m --region us-west-2 --min-duration 300s --output table
- If sessions are "stuck" (clients disconnected but server retains session): mark for reclamation.

3) Reclaim tokens (safe reclamation)

- Goal: free stranded KV references and close dangling streams without impacting healthy sessions.
- Command (example): redwood operator tokens reclaim --shard <shard-id> --dry-run
- Inspect dry-run output. If safe, run: redwood operator tokens reclaim --shard <shard-id> --force --reason "operator-reclaim-<INC_ID>"
- Consequence: reclaimed tokens will be reported as reclaimed in token-forensics and should reduce reported in-use GPU time.

4) Trigger targeted cache compaction and integrity check

- Action: Run a cache integrity job to remove orphaned KV entries and compact prefix indexes.
- Command (example): redwood runtime cache-integrity run --shard <shard-id> --level compact --max-io 50MB/s
- Expected outcome: immediate reclaim of memory and improved hit-rate on subsequent requests.

5) Controlled warm-up (gradual traffic replay pattern)

- Rationale: Full fan-out warmups are expensive and can overshoot burst budget. Use staged synthetic or low-priority replay.
- Steps:
  a) Schedule a low-QPS synthetic replay: redwood replay start --shard <shard-id> --template warmup-small --qps 2 --duration 10m --tag operator-warmup-<INC_ID>
  b) After 10m, measure cache-hit-rate and latency. If hit-rate improves >= 15 percentage points and P99 improves, increase to qps 8 for 15m.
  c) Continue incremental increases until baseline reached or budget exhausted.
- Safety: replay traffic must be tagged and rate-limited. Reject or pause replay if GPU utilization climbs > 85% or cost burn nears cap.

6) Post-warmup verification

- Verify: cache-hit-rate at pre-incident baseline, P50/P95/P99 latencies back to expected ranges, token-session counts normalized.
- Commands: redwood telemetry metrics get --metric kv_cache_hit_rate --shard <shard-id> --window 5m

Safe fallback and rollback procedures

- If synthetic warmup causes degradation or cost runaway: immediately stop all replay jobs: redwood replay stop --tag operator-warmup-<INC_ID>
- If reclamation caused client disruption (rare): restore token state via token-snapshot rollback if snapshot exists: redwood operator tokens rollback --snapshot <snapshot-id> --shard <shard-id>. Contact serving-runtime on-call before running rollback.

Longer-term remediation (after immediate fix)

- Run an automated job to pre-warm cache for low-traffic tenants during predictable windows (off-peak).
- Add hysteresis to token lifetime detection to avoid premature reclamation.
- Update routing policy to prefer warm shards for high-latency-sensitive routes for the first 30 mins after regional failover.

Operator checklist (to paste in incident ticket)

- [ ] Confirm affected shard IDs and tenants
- [ ] Retrieve token-session snapshot (pre-action)
- [ ] Run token reclaim dry-run and capture output
- [ ] Execute reclaim (if safe) and note command/flags
- [ ] Start controlled warmup (tag with incident number)
- [ ] Monitor key metrics for 60 minutes post-reclaim
- [ ] Stop warmup and record cost delta
- [ ] Create postmortem ticket if root cause unknown or if SLOs not restored within 90 minutes

Templates and example incident annotations

- Incident note (one-line): "Token reclamation + targeted warmup for shard s-0452 — reclaimed 1.1m stranded tokens; cache hit-rate recovered from 12% -> 71% in 42m; P99 returned to 240ms"
- Ticket snippet: "Commands executed: tokens reclaim --shard s-0452 --force --reason operator-reclaim-INC-2027-012; replay start --shard s-0452 --template warmup-small --qps 2 --duration 10m --tag operator-warmup-INC-2027-012"

Post-run analysis and retro triggers

- Metrics to capture: pre/post kv_cache_hit_rate, P50/P95/P99 latency deltas, GPU-hours consumed, cost delta, number of reclaimed tokens, list of affected tenants.
- Retro triggers (create a retrospective if any of the following):
  - SLO not restored within 90 minutes
  - Cost delta > configured budget without prior approval
  - Repeated occurrence for same shard or tenant within 30 days

Appendix A — recommended dashboard queries

- KV cache hit-rate (per-shard):
  query: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_lookups[5m])) by (shard)
- Token session duration distribution:
  query: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_session_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant))
- Synthetic warmup job CPU/GPU throttle check:
  query: max_over_time(gpu_utilization[5m]) by (shard)

Appendix B — safe-parameter reference

| Parameter | Default | Rationale |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| warmup_qps_initial | 2 | conservative start to avoid sudden load spikes |
| warmup_step_qps | 4 | incremental increase per stage |
| warmup_max_gpu_util | 85% | throttling threshold to avoid contention |
| reclaim_dry_run | true | always validate results before forcing |
| burst_cost_cap | $500 | emergency budget per region (configurable) |

Related improvements backlog (examples)

- Automate token leak detection to create auto-PRs for suspected client SDKs with long-lived sessions.
- Add safe, cluster-level pre-warm schedules for low-traffic shards.
- Expose per-tenant warmup budgets and automated approval flows.

Contacts and escalation directory

- Serving Runtime on-call: see rotation page /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/oncall-rotation.json

End of playbook
